lessons.title: portare — "to carry," and what an Italian does with a coat
lessons.gloss: to carry, to bring — and, without warning, to wear

segments.text: Chapter 19 closed on a verb that ran backwards — mi piace il vino, where the wine does the pleasing and you are only the one it happens to. Here is a plain one: the -are endings of aiuto, aiuti, aiuta, doing a job English splits three ways.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the word

segments.text: portare — to carry, to bring, to take along.
Porto il pane. — I bring the bread. Porto l'acqua. — I bring the water. Porto il vino. — I bring the wine.
Hold it against prendere, which was seizing — what you reach out and pick up. Portare is what happens next: the thing travels with you.
A second job catches learners out. This same verb also means to wear. Clothes are things you carry on your person, so porto covers a coat as readily as a loaf.
portare comes from Latin portāre, "to carry." English is stacked with it:
portable; porter, who carries your bags; portfolio, from Italian portafoglio, a leaf-carrier.
transport ("carry across"), export ("carry out"), import ("carry in"), report ("carry back"), support, deport.
sport — nobody sees this one coming. Old French desporter meant "to carry away": the mind, from serious matters. English wore disport down to sport.
Two cautions. The harbour port is a different Latin word, portus. And Latin manus, which gave you la mano, sits in the phrase a mano, "by hand": the hand is what does the carrying.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the endings, and a participle that behaves

segments.text: Drop -are, add the usual: porto, porti, porta.
Chapter 15 gave you ho plus a participle; Chapters 18 and 19 handed you three that would not sit still. This one behaves:

utterances: verb: portare. participle: portato. with ho: ho portato — I brought.
verb: scrivere. participle: scritto. with ho: ho scritto — I wrote.
verb: prendere. participle: preso. with ho: ho preso — I took.

segments.text: Every regular -are participle ends in -ato. Scritto doubled its t because scriptum had a cluster to resolve; preso lost an n because prehēnsum had one to lose. Portāre had neither.

segments.text: Bring the wine. (Porto il vino.) What did portāre mean, and name three English cousins. (To carry; transport, export, import, porter.) Which English word for games is this verb in disguise? (Sport, from desporter, "to carry away".) Give the participle, and say why it is not doubled like scritto. (Portato; portāre had no cluster to collapse.) What else does portare mean? (To wear.)

lessons.title: comprare — "to buy," and the false trail to "compare"
lessons.gloss: to buy — from procuring, not from comparing, however much the two look alike

segments.text: A second -are verb, so the endings cost you nothing. What is new is the root, which sends nearly every English speaker down the wrong road on sight.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the word

segments.text: comprare — to buy.
Compro il pane. — I buy the bread. Compro l'acqua. — I buy the water. Compro il vino. — I buy the wine.
Italian keeps a longer form too, comperare. That is the older shape; speech squeezed the middle e out. Both are real, and the short one is what you hear.

comprare comes from Latin comparāre, and the verb underneath it is parāre, "to make ready, to procure." Put com-, "together," in front and buying is procuring: bringing the thing and the price into one place. English took parāre over and over:
prepare (prae-, "beforehand"), repair (re-, "back into readiness"), separate (sē-, "apart").
apparatus and apparel — things made ready, for a machine and for a body.
emperor and empire, through imperāre, which is in- plus this same parāre.
Italian's own parare, "to ward off," borrowed as parry and standing in parasol and parachute.
English compare looks like a free gift here. It is not: the resemblance is exact and the connection is nil. Latin had two verbs spelled comparāre, built on unrelated words:

utterances: Latin verb: comparāre (procure). built on: parāre, "make ready". where it went: Italian comprare, to buy.
Latin verb: comparāre (match). built on: pār, "equal". where it went: English compare.

segments.text: The second is the pār of par, parity, peer, pair and umpire: setting two things side by side as equals. Buying is procuring, not weighing up.
Spanish comprar and Portuguese comprar took the procuring-verb Italian took; French abandoned it and buys with acheter.
Chapter 5's exercise still works, with more to chew on. Take each -are verb through io / tu / lui-lei:
parlare: parlo, parli, parla.
portare: porto, porti, porta.
comprare: compro, compri, compra.
Same three endings, -o / -i / -a, and the pronoun stays dropped. The past is regular: ho comprato il pane.

segments.instruction: the warning — "comprare is procuring, not comparing"

segments.text: Buy the bread. (Compro il pane.) Which Latin verb is inside comprare? (Parāre — to make ready, to procure.) Name three English cousins. (Prepare, repair, separate, apparatus, emperor.) Why is English compare not a relative? (Different Latin verb, same spelling, built on pār, "equal".) And which verb from the last lesson meant "to carry"? (Portare.)

lessons.title: aspettare — "to wait," which began as "to watch"
lessons.gloss: to wait — and, with one small word in front, to expect

segments.text: A third -are verb. Its endings are free, its root is one of the most productive in English, and the doubled tt in the middle is the work of a sound-law you learned while counting to ten.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the word

segments.text: aspettare — to wait, to wait for.
Aspetto. — I'm waiting. Aspetto Anna. — I'm waiting for Anna. Aspetto Marco. — I'm waiting for Marco.
Notice what the Italian is missing: any word meaning for. English cannot "wait somebody." Italian takes the person straight, as porto il pane takes the bread.

aspettare comes from Latin spectāre, "to watch, to gaze at", with ad-, "toward," welded on the front: to watch toward something. Waiting is watching for a thing to arrive, and the root runs through English:
spectator, spectacle, spectacles, spectrum.
inspect ("look into"), respect ("look back at"), prospect ("look forward"), suspect ("look from underneath"), aspect.
species and specimen, from the plain verb specere, "to look."

Classical Latin's own word for waiting was exspectāre — ex- plus that same verb, "to watch out for" — and English took that one and made it expect. So wait and expect are one Latin verb wearing two prefixes, and Italian's single aspettare stands on the ground of both.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the doubled t, and the word that narrows the meaning

segments.text: Present: aspetto, aspetti, aspetta. Past: ho aspettato, regular.
First that tt. Latin spectāre carries -ct-, and you know what Italian does with -ct-: octō became otto, lectum letto, scriptum scritto. The same law gives aspettare.
Second, the narrowing. Put mi in front and the verb stops meaning wait and starts meaning expect:

That mi is a word you have met working elsewhere. In mi chiamo it turned the verb back on you — "I call myself." In mi piace it named the person a thing is pleasing to. Here it turns outward watching into inward reckoning.

segments.text: Say you are waiting for Anna. (Aspetto Anna — nothing for "for".) What did spectāre mean, and name three English cousins. (To watch; spectator, inspect, respect, prospect, species.) Which prefix gave English expect, and which gave Italian aspettare? (Ex- and ad-.) Why the doubled tt, and what does mi aspetto mean? (-ct- collapses to -tt-, as in otto; I expect.)

lessons.title: incontrare — "to meet," which is literally "to come against"
lessons.gloss: to meet — literally "to come against", with a second meeting-verb hiding inside a past tense

segments.text: The chapter's last -are verb. Its root is a preposition, its past settles a question Chapter 16 left open, and Italian keeps a second meeting-verb that shows its meaning only in the past.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the word

segments.text: incontrare — to meet, to run into. incontro, incontri, incontra.
Incontro Marco. — I meet Marco. Incontro Anna. — I meet Anna.
It has a partner English cannot keep apart from it, conoscere. Incontrare is the event, two people in one place; conoscere is the acquaintance, knowing a person.

incontrare from Late Latin incontrā: in- plus contrā, "against, opposite." To meet somebody is to come against them — not a fight, a facing. English borrowed it through French as encounter; bare contrā gave contrary, contrast, counter.
The best of the family is country: Vulgar Latin named a region (terra) contrāta, "the land lying opposite" — what is in front of you when you turn from the town.
conoscere is a different house: Latin cognōscere, co- plus gnōscere, "to come to know" becomes cognition, recognize, incognito, notice.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: which past, and the one that means "met"

segments.text: Chapter 16 split the past in two. Motion and change take essere, and the participle agrees: Marco è andato, Anna è andata, sono stato. All else takes avere, and nothing agrees.
Ho incontrato Marco. — I met Marco. Ho incontrato Anna. — I met Anna.
Two people, one unmoved incontrato — because after essere the participle began as an adjective describing the subject, and after avere it describes nobody.
Now the hidden verb. Put conoscere in the past and its job changes:
Ho conosciuto Marco. — I met Marco — for the first time.
portare from portāre, "carry" becomes transport, export, porter, sport; it also means to wear, and portato is the regular participle.
comprare from comparāre on parāre, "procure" becomes prepare, repair, apparatus — and not the comparāre behind English compare.
aspettare from ad- + spectāre, "watch toward" becomes spectator, inspect, prospect; ex- on that verb gave expect, and mi aspetto says it.
incontrare from in- + contrā, "against" becomes encounter, contrary, country.

The thread: four verbs, one set of -are endings — porto, compro, aspetto, incontro — and three of them weld a small word onto a plain Latin verb: com-, ad-, in-. Italian inherited the welds without the seams.
